#43973. Latest Update: How I’m Approaching AI Search (And How You Should To)

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2829 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How I’m Approaching AI Search (And How You Should To)

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in focusing on citation tactics and cheap visibility tricks, we’re missing the bigger picture.
  • Sources indicate that there’s nothing inherently wrong with it.
  • I don’t have the energy or the wherewithal to play catch-up every year or two.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI is strangely simple. And we’re overcomplicating it.

It has been revealed that in focusing on citation tactics and cheap visibility tricks, we’re missing the bigger picture. As an industry, we’ve got away with poor content for years. Updating the same “best spoons” article three times a week because some other idiot is doing exactly the same thing.

Sources indicate that there’s nothing inherently wrong with it. It’s just too SEO-y. We’re missing a much bigger opportunity by framing it through a really narrow lens.

I don’t have the energy or the wherewithal to play catch-up every year or two. So I think of AI search as the ultimate synthesis of your marketing efforts.

Your positioning, reputation, expertise, content, and presence across the internet are all potential inputs into how AI systems understand and represent you.

It’s not just about your website anymore.

I’ve spent a lot of time recently working on AI search, information retrieval, audience research, and discoverability strategies. The more I do, the more convinced I become that we need to approach this as marketers, not SEOs.

In a recent development, but don’t build your entire “marketing” strategy around it. I use marketing in the loosest possible sense of the word.

If you’re in dire need of a refresher, here’s a few parts on the fundamentals of modern information retrieval:.

In a recent development, there’s one other concept I haven’t written about in detail: query fan-out. Not because it’s not important, more just because a) it’s pretty dull and b) it isn’t a new concept for SEOs. We’ve been using tools like AlsoAsked for years to understand related questions, adjacent information needs and the wider context surrounding a search.

Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

But we also need to distinguish between three things:.

They’re related, but they aren’t interchangeable. Being crawled doesn’t guarantee inclusion in training data. Being retrieved doesn’t guarantee a citation. And a citation doesn’t guarantee commercial value.

Understanding these mechanisms is crucial – mainly just so you can answer the brain-dead questions people ask you about AI. Building your entire marketing strategy around their current implementation is the action of a halfwit.

According to recent reports, models, retrieval systems, and interfaces will change. An owned audience is a considerably more durable investment. So build one.

Sources indicate that this is the biggest change I’ve made to my approach. Not just for AI search, but for traditional SEO.

Industry observers note that I don’t begin by asking which prompts a brand should appear in. Or how much search volume a keyword or even topic has. Mainly because my trust in search volume and all forms of visibility is at rock bottom.

So I use SparkToro to investigate where audiences spend time, which websites they visit, who influences them, and which platforms they’re disproportionately likely to use compared with the wider population.

For this audience, I know that if I want to influence them, LinkedIn is a non-negotiable (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

I combine that with traditional search research, AI search behaviour and an assessment of the brand’s existing positioning. You don’t need to overcomplicate this – ask a number of different LLMs about insert brand and record the responses.

I want to answer some relatively straightforward questions:.

This research should inform two things.

It has been revealed that first, our owned platforms. We use what we’ve learned to improve the way we position ourselves, the services we offer, the language we use, and the content we create.

Let’s try to make things under our control as human and well-targeted as possible.

Second, our wider marketing strategy. We identify the publications, communities, creators, platforms, and people capable of influencing that audience, and decide how to reach them.

Audience affinity with specific Subreddits, via SparkToro (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

Industry observers note that you need to know this. Not because it might get your brand mentioned as part of the training data. But because this is where you should be marketing.

Made-up prompt data is out. Real, human-led marketing is in. If we want SEO to be taken seriously, this is the proper evolution.

The goal isn’t to manufacture mentions for an AI model. It’s to build a brand people want to discover, engage with, and recommend.

If those activities also increase your representation in AI systems, wonderful. But that’s a delicious byproduct, not the reason for doing them.

In a recent development, while audience research informs the wider strategy, your website needs to be accessible, understandable, and representative of who you are. That is something reasonably competent SEOs can lead.

Can the relevant search and AI crawlers access your content? Can they render it? Are you inadvertently blocking systems you want to reach?

This means reviewing bot management, robots directives, rendering, indexability, internal linking, site architecture, and the usual technical SEO fundamentals.

A traditional SEO-type audit with a few improvements.

One that understands that not all AI bots serve the same purpose. Training crawlers, search crawlers, and user-triggered retrieval systems can have different access requirements and commercial implications.

Crawlers do different things (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

It has been revealed that especially important if you’re working for – or with – a publisher. Someone whose business may depend on you understanding the wider context.

If you’re restricting access to your content, you need to understand what you’re giving up, what you’re protecting, and where the value might exist instead.

Perhaps that’s content licensing, direct audience relationships or proprietary products.

Sources indicate that the role of the SEO changes considerably in an environment where you’re not maximising access. You’re helping the business understand the trade-offs between visibility, intellectual property and commercial value.

It has been revealed that it’s like a paywall. You’re restricting reach for commercial purposes. It’s the correct move if played properly.

See Cyrus Shepherd’s excellent test to understand how much search traffic was truly influenced by Google’s AI proposition.

Sources indicate that this is where I think modern information retrieval methods and SEO intersect perfectly. I’ve written about how to approach this in Entities Are the Foundation of Modern SEO.

This framework is relatively simple:.

Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t about adding some structured data and hoping ChatGPT tries to hump your leg. Spoiler: It won’t.

It’s about making sure that your owned presence accurately represents your positioning and that the wider internet provides credible, independent evidence to support it.

So, we know who we are. We’ve represented ourselves properly. Now we have to rely on *shudders* other people to corroborate this message.

We have to build an off-site presence.

This references a podcast I did with Andy Francos and an article I wrote for Lumar two years ago (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

We’re talking actual, real marketing (not SEO). PR, partnerships, content and audience development.

If the people you’re trying to reach spend their time reading particular publications, following particular experts or participating in particular communities, those are the places worth investing in.

Bollocks to a citation. Your audience is there. You know, people you could actually sell something to.

That might mean publishing original research, collaborating with influential people, appearing on podcasts, creating genuinely useful resources or contributing expertise to relevant publications.

Some of those activities will generate links. Others will generate mentions, relationships, conversations and brand demand – a real representation of site quality in Google.

The more consistently you’re associated with the right subjects, people and organizations, the stronger your wider digital presence can become. That is, in essence, how training data and entity relationships work.

Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

If you’re lucky, some of that evidence may eventually influence how AI systems represent you.

But you won’t care, because you’ll have been making sales by marketing to actual customers.

Modern methods of information retrieval across SEO and AI search share many, if not all of the same fundamentals.

Arguably, AI search has a longer tail to it. But it’s not sustainable, nor sensible, to create a page for every possible thought your audience may have. To perpetuate a false Henry Ford quote:.

“If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses.” H. Ford, Never.

So you need to strike a balance. No one cares about visibility without impact. At least not for long.

There is room to try and test things. Good things. Things real people will care about.

People like Jan-Willem Bobbink and Dan Petrovic highlight some really brilliant things you can test that are eminently sensible for SEO and AI search. Surprise, surprise, they work for people too. It’s marketing.

Let me give you an example. Maybe more accurately, let me steal one of Jan’s:.

Sources indicate that “I spent the last three weeks on SEO / GEO work for B2B clients, and the changes that made the biggest difference were mostly about information that was missing or hard to find. Buyers run into the same problems on these sites, so you can usually get these fixes approved without having to explain SEO to anyone.”.

Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett.

Recent findings suggest that being explicit, consistent, and accurate is not an AI hack. It’s just pretty sensible.

It has been revealed that adding pricing pages, case studies, and telling people why you are the best in the business are always good ideas. Even if your pricing pages just say something like prices starting at x, that is a better way of finding the right audience.

And if you want to feature in AI responses, for god’s sake don’t hide your case studies. You need to provide a clear reason for your inclusion. Hard if your best work is hidden.

Statements like “Client Y saw a 30% improvement in deliverability metrics” can noticeably improve your citation rate because a model is literally looking for a reason to include you. You need to give them one. Just as you would a person.

In a recent development, experience. Expertise. Authority. Trust. Not so stupid after all.

According to recent reports, measurement’s been broken for a decade anyway. It’s just nice for the C-suite to have numbers to report on – even if they’re complete hokum.

You try and figure this out (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

AI visibility’s not much better. A hugely flawed metric given the personalization, lack of prompt data, and completely individual prompts. But it’s better than nothing. Indicative at best, but you need to use something.

People still want to know how they’re represented in AI systems. And so they should – it’s a valuable channel. My preference is to establish a representative set of prompts across four areas:.

Track these consistently across the systems that matter to your audience.

Look at whether you’re mentioned, how you’re described, which competitors appear, and which sources are being used. Find out when you start to appear for certain terms and see if it matches your positioning.

I always track my mentions with Alertmouse (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

I appear in AI recommendations around news SEO expertise despite having done nothing specifically to optimize for AI search.

What I have done is spend years working in the industry, publishing, building relationships, contributing expertise, and establishing a reasonably clear on-site and off-site identity.

Not a bad list, although I am not sure ChatGPT is quite nailing the profile pictures for us… (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett).

I guarantee you, if you ask Barry Adams, he’ll tell you he’s done nothing special for AI either.

In a recent development, I’ve written what I think are high-quality articles on third-party websites and podcasts, featured in roundups, and built my own distribution platform. It just also happens to work for featuring in AI systems.

Industry observers note that AI systems don’t necessarily need to send you traffic to influence commercial outcomes. Which is a good thing, because ChatGPT sends less than 1% of Google’s traffic.

Similarweb’s research found that people who received a brand recommendation in ChatGPT were 2.5 times more likely to visit that brand’s website within the following seven days than users who were recommended a competitor.

Recent findings suggest that much of that activity happened through subsequent branded searches rather than direct AI referrals. One of those measures of site quality that should be monitored.

In a recent development, AI search can and does function as a brand discovery and consideration channel. I think referral traffic is, at best, a secondary measure of success from LLMs. While they’ve engineered the exit out, you cannot deny the reach these systems have.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, our attribution systems can’t cope with “I saw it here once.” We need to focus on incremental change. The outcomes attributable to marketing.

Industry observers note that establish a baseline. Run a campaign. Measure changes in branded demand, direct visits, conversions, leads, and commercial outcomes. Compare with appropriate benchmarks or control groups where possible.

Keep tracking AI visibility, referrals and citations, but use them as supporting indicators.

Our objective is to establish whether said marketing activity is creating additional business value, not whether ChatGPT has linked to your homepage.

For businesses whose models depend on monetizing information and attracting a click, AI search presents a very different challenge.

They are monetizing other people’s work for their own ill-gotten gain. That is an irrefutable commercial dilemma. Hence all the protectionism. So we need to establish what that cost is and try to find alternative methods of monetization.

In The Generative AI Report Sucks – Let’s Make It Brilliant, I outlined how publishers can combine AI visibility data with traffic dependency, commercial value, audience resilience, and server logs.

We can go some way toward solving actual business problems.

Always, always, always a good thing to do. Regardless of your job.

In a recent development, this opportunity is no different, especially for organizations (like publishers) with substantial authority across particular subjects. They have influence within the wider information ecosystem.

That influence can have commercial value.

Recent findings suggest that publishers Should Think About AI Visibility. Content licensing, data partnerships, research collaborations, and other commercial arrangements offer opportunities to monetize expertise and proprietary information.

But this needs careful handling.

Recent findings suggest that selling links or undisclosed editorial influence is not a sustainable AI strategy. It introduces reputational, editorial, and search-policy risks.

The more sustainable opportunity is to understand the value of your existing content, expertise, audience, and distribution – and build legitimate commercial products around those assets.

Lots of companies are selling or actively considering selling their archived assets or data to AI companies:.

For publishers in particular, this is an opportunity to rethink the value they create beyond the click. See the Daily Mail’s approach to GEO monetization here.

According to recent reports, if you’re more on the glass half full side, you’ll be able to sniff out commercial opportunities. Ideally ones that don’t ruin the brand or fall foul of Google’s link payment guidelines.

General advice: If something smells a bit off, it probably is.

If you’re a business looking to take this seriously, there’s an organizational question you need to answer.

Who is responsible for all of this?

Because as great as we can be, it shouldn’t just be your SEO.

This touches technical infrastructure, audience research, brand positioning, content, PR, distribution, commercial partnerships, and measurement. That requires someone who understands the entire ecosystem and, crucially, how to influence people.

Nobody is an expert at all of these things. They’re too different. Too complex.

In a recent development, for larger businesses, I’d be thinking about a Head of Marketing or Head of Discoverability with responsibility for coordinating these activities. Someone who at least knows the basics of each and can herd a clowder of cats.

They need the authority to bring different teams together, allocate resources, challenge existing assumptions and measure outcomes against business objectives.

There’s a reason SEOs rarely graduate to marketing lead positions. We don’t understand wider marketing because we’ve rarely had to. SEO was always the best channel… According to wonky data, anyway.

AI search gives us a very good reason to change that.

And for anyone working in SEO, I think there are three particularly interesting directions.

All three have tremendous value. Limiting yourself to SEO, particularly as a collection of search-engine or LLM-specific tactics, is increasingly short-sighted.

Discoverability has been changing for a decade. We need to think much more broadly about how audiences discover and engage with content. The opportunity is to bring those disciplines together.

A little rebrand and refocus on what you want from your career may be the best thing you ever do.

According to recent reports, stop trying to engineer your way into an AI response. Build a brand worth recommending, an audience worth owning, and a business that benefits whether the citation comes or not.

Recent findings suggest that enjoy yourself. This will be a better era for marketers and marketing. Your competition is lazy and inept. They’re just faster.

Elon Musk’s Grokipedia is littered with mistakes. But Wikipedia could still learn some things from it.

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
  • It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to .
  • Grokipedia reveals that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

Nearly there — check your email.

It has been revealed that we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Grokipedia reveals that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet.

When I saw Grokipedia’s articles about me, the memories came rushing back: my 19 years in minor league baseball, including that impressive season with the Montgomery Rebels when I hit 20 home runs. I was lean back then — 6 feet tall and 168 pounds — and earned a career batting average just under .300. I became a minor league coach and managed the Chicago White Sox for a short stint in 1970, which Grokipedia said “highlighted [my] readiness for higher-level responsibilities.”.

I then attended Arizona State University, switched to a career in journalism, created the fact-checking site PolitiFact, won a Pulitzer Prize, and now teach journalism at Duke University.

Ah, the memories!…except that I never played minor league baseball, never managed the White Sox, and can only dream about being 6 feet tall. (I’m 5’8″.) Grokipedia, the AI-written encyclopedia of Elon Musk, has confused me with Marion Danne “Bill” Adair, who died in 2002.

Recent findings suggest that that article and another one about “Bill Adair (journalist)” — which really is me — illustrate the many flaws of Grokipedia, which launched a year ago. The articles are littered with mistakes and superfluous details. They are terribly written and ridiculously long. If Grok, the AI engine that wrote this turgid prose, were a student in one of my writing courses, I would give it a D. (Editor’s note: After this article was published, someone updated the inaccurate Grok pages. The original versions are linked here.).

According to recent reports, still, the articles provide valuable lessons for Wikipedia editors who are debating how and when to use AI. Grokipedia adds latest content and context that Wikipedia often lacks. It reveals that AI is actually pretty good at finding tidbits in the far corners of the internet and summarizing them in sweeping prose. It can also provide balance to articles that need it.

Grok can’t write worth a lick, but it shows how Wikipedia can take advantage of AI at a time when overworked editors are trying to keep the encyclopedia alive.

Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he remarked was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet. With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a latest version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.” When Grokipedia launched, Musk said he had substantial aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video. Maybe someday. For now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia highlights edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make. Last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk. Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors revealed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok said I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too quickly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a big scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s important and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. Bernadette Meehan, CEO of the Wikimedia Foundation, which provides money and technical infrastructure for the encyclopedia, has called AI “an existential threat” to Wikipedia. Musk launched Grokipedia as an alternative to Wikipedia, which he stated was too liberal. (He called it “Wokepedia.”) Still, he trusted it enough to have Grok copy hundreds of thousands of its articles, which is permitted under Wikipedia’s Creative Commons license, and then add content from elsewhere on the internet.

With his usual bluster, Musk said his encyclopedia used a latest version of his large language model that was good at “cogent analysis.” He said programmers told it to “cycle through the million most popular articles in Wikipedia and add, modify, and delete.”.

According to recent reports, when Grokipedia released, Musk said he had substantial aspirations to overtake Wikipedia, which has 68 million articles in more than 300 languages. He said his encyclopedia would be more complete and more balanced and would make smarter use of images and video.

In a recent development, for now, Grokipedia is a massive collection of overly long articles that are often out of date. Its flaws have been well-documented: Articles are littered with mistakes, peddle conspiracy theories, rely on low-credibility sources, and sometimes skew to the right. And although Grokipedia indicates edit requests from readers and whether they are approved, the site is not as transparent as Wikipedia, which reveals details about its editors and every change they make.

According to recent reports, last spring, Grokipedia mysteriously stopped updating, according to a report by researchers Renée DiResta and Ronald Robertson. It resumed in late September, still a hot mess, but with a more colorful homepage that always seems to feature its article about Musk.

Grokipedia has two articles about me: the conflated baseball player one and “Bill Adair (journalist),” the real one, which is incredibly boring, even to me. Both borrow heavily from Wikipedia’s articles about us and enrich them with details found on assorted websites. Wikipedia’s article about me is nicely concise — just 700 words. It is written in the encyclopedia’s signature dry style and doesn’t contain any errors. The article recounts my career, some of the major news events I’ve covered, the two books I’ve written, and the awards I’ve won. But it highlights trivial events from my career, fails to emphasize larger ones, and lacks any criticism of my work. (I have not tried to improve the article because Wikipedia’s conflict of interest policy prohibits people from editing their own bios.) By contrast, Grokipedia’s “Bill Adair (journalist)” is painfully long — 5,600 words. Its greatest value would be to help someone suffering from a sleep disorder. Like a college student trying to meet a word count, Grok stuffed the article with needless details and redundant descriptions. The article tells you about my work with PolitiFact and then tells you again and again. It explains the site’s rating scale eight times and mentions my academic title four times. Despite labels that say “fact-checked by Grok,” both articles had lots of errors. I spotted 32 in the journalist one and so many in the baseball mashup that I couldn’t count them all. Mistakes are not surprising in AI writing, but I discovered interesting patterns that reveal the weaknesses of large language models. In the article about the real me, only seven of the errors were hallucinations in which Grok seemed to create a detail out of thin air. No, I did not win an award from Manhattan College, and no, PolitiFact did not begin by fact-checking the Tampa mayor’s race. Five other errors showed Grok was a lazy researcher that did not look broadly enough to check a claim. Grok noted I am the director of Duke’s journalism program, but I left that job five years ago. The sources cited in the article don’t explain Grok’s mistake, so it seems likely it remembered an old announcement and failed to see a newer one that named my successor. The most prevalent errors were in a broad category I’d all cluelessness. These mistakes showed Grok didn’t fully understand what it read, like someone who skimmed an article too rapidly. My favorite in this category was when I got credit for a major scoop in 2000 that George W. Bush had a DUI conviction, which the Grokipedia article said had an impact on “late-election discourse.” I wish! Yes, I was among the many journalists who covered that story, but I had no scoop. Together, the errors reveal that Grok is a knucklehead. It doesn’t know what’s crucial and what’s not. It is simply mashing together details from many web articles about me. Grok only knows what it found on the internet and it lacks experience and perspective to sort out what’s important. The writing is dreadful. The articles read as if Grok was trained on too many online resumes and corporate memos. Grok uses words and phrases like “commenced” and “transitioned” and “multidisciplinary practicum” and “hypotheses on fact-check efficacy.” A typical sentence: “Adair’s approach in this position reflected a commitment to undiluted sourcing and causal analysis of policy impacts, influencing subsequent innovations in political journalism.” Take a close look at that sentence and you’ll see it’s just a mush of buzzwords. I don’t know what “undiluted sourcing” is and have never used the phrase, nor would I refer to “causal analysis”…of anything. Grok is trying to impress us with an MBA vocabulary but is really just an epic bullshitter. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, microsoft Advertising is rolling out what it calls its biggest bidding model upgrade in a decade.
  • According to recent reports, microsoft will apply the upgrade automatically as it reaches more accounts.
  • In a recent development, microsoft claims the newly introduced models can change how swiftly campaigns spend and how closely they stick to your targets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, microsoft Advertising is rolling out what it calls its biggest bidding model upgrade in a decade. The newly introduced models use more signals to predict whether an ad click will turn into a conversion and what it might be worth.

According to recent reports, microsoft will apply the upgrade automatically as it reaches more accounts. That means campaigns can start spending differently before you make any changes yourself. Microsoft confirmed the rollout on November 18 and intends more bidding updates in 2027.

In a recent development, microsoft claims the newly introduced models can change how swiftly campaigns spend and how closely they stick to your targets. These are the areas to keep an eye on:.

A $50 CPA target still leaves room for a campaign to bring in conversions at $40 each, even if it spends its full budget. A max CPC can limit that flexibility. Say you average $3 a click and cap bids at $5. The cap rules out a $6 bid even if Microsoft expects the click could bring in a conversion within your CPA target.

Sources indicate that say you raise your CPA target on Monday and customers usually take a week to buy. By Friday, you know what Monday’s clicks cost, but you may still be waiting on some of the sales. Faster bidding won’t shorten the time those customers take to buy.

Raising a CPA target or lowering a ROAS target can open up auctions your campaign previously passed up. To limit swings in performance, Microsoft suggests making those changes in 15% increments and reviewing each after one conversion cycle. For a bigger change, like switching bid strategies or adding a conversion goal, Microsoft recommends allowing one to two cycles.

According to recent reports, microsoft recommends conversion-based bidding for fresh campaigns once the account has at least five conversions. Those can come from campaigns you already run. If you’re still gathering your first five, Enhanced CPC is an option.

On LinkedIn, Sophie Westall asked if the same advice applies to low-volume accounts already using Enhanced CPC. Microsoft Advertising Liaison Navah Hopkins replied:.

Every account is different so a blanket recommendation still needs to be put to the test. With that mentioned, so long as the account has at least 5 conversions total, the system is smart enough to use that to begin with conversion-based bidding. While we still recommend the 30-day evaluation period and not making too many changes if you’re working with fewer conversions, the system is much more responsive now!

Sources indicate that for judging performance, Microsoft recommends around 30 conversions in 30 days at the campaign or portfolio level. A low-volume campaign can reach the end of that first month and still have too few conversions to judge the switch.

Microsoft reported 10% more conversion value per click at roughly the same ROAS after the model upgrade. That result came from August 2026 global Search and Audience Network data for advertisers using Maximize Conversion Value or Target ROAS.

Industry observers note that microsoft also looked at advertisers who switched bid strategies. Search advertisers who moved from Target CPA to Target ROAS saw 8% more conversion value at a similar ROAS. Advertisers who moved from Enhanced CPC to Maximize Conversions with a CPA target saw 18% more conversions at a similar CPA.

If you’re considering Target ROAS, pull up a few recent purchases in Microsoft Advertising and compare the reported values with the order totals. A $40 order and a $400 order can both show up as conversions even if your tracking assigns them the same value. That’s easy to miss if you’re used to checking that purchases are coming through and leaving it there.

According to recent reports, microsoft reported its largest gains from value-based bidding among advertisers who sent actual transaction values. If your purchase goal uses a fixed value, the reported ROAS reflects that estimate. It can move as you sell more or spend less, but it won’t capture a change in how much customers spend per order.

Industry observers note that with lead gen, you may need time to get a better read on what a conversion is worth. Two people can submit the same form, and sales may find out a week later that only one is a fit.

It has been revealed that pedro Bailaderia asked Navah Hopkins about sending an estimate at submission and updating it once more information comes into the CRM. Hopkins supported using the Conversions API or offline imports. She also advised setting a ROAS target that reflects the values you send.

In a recent development, if your team is still working out how to value a qualified lead, that’s worth settling before you set a ROAS target. A campaign can hit the target you set while sales is still waiting for more leads it can work with.

If a campaign already brings in the sales or leads you need at a cost you’re happy with, you can give the upgrade some room before changing anything. Keeping your settings steady makes it easier to see how the new models work with the goals and budget you already have.

Industry observers note that the rollout may be more useful if you’ve been adjusting targets to get a campaign to spend more evenly. If delivery settles down on its own, you may have fewer reasons to touch those targets during the week. That would leave you freer to change them when the business needs more volume or can afford to pay more for a conversion.

Sources indicate that hi there! We're hiring an Information Security Engineer with a focus on Application Security to join our Information Security team at Camunda.

We are a team that takes security seriously without making it feel like a locked door. We work in a transparent, straightforward way, and we care about doing the work right rather than just checking a compliance box.

You will work side by side with our R&D engineers: reviewing designs, threat modeling new features, digging into code and helping teams make good, risk-based decisions about the vulnerabilities that come in. You'll also help build the internal tools that make this work scale, including our CVE registry and the LLM-assisted workflows we use to analyse code and triage findings.

Camunda is an AI-first organization, and InfoSec is no exception: AI agents are part of how we review code, assess vulnerabilities, and build our tools. You will help shape how that works.

Sources indicate that this is a hands-on role for someone who already has solid AppSec foundations and wants to grow. We are a generalist team, so you will also take part in our on-call rotation and incident response, and get exposure to other areas of security. But most of your time will be spent with engineers and building and maintaining internal tools and processes.

Vulnerability management: triage findings from SCA, container and code scanning, external reports and internal security testing; assess whether Camunda is actually affected; agree fix / mitigate / accept with engineering and follow through to release.

Threat modeling and security reviews: run threat modeling sessions and design reviews with R&D teams for latest features and architecture changes, and turn the results into concrete, prioritised actions.

Code analysis with LLMs: use and improve LLM-assisted tooling (agents, prompts, reusable skills) to review code, validate findings and reproduce issues, while applying your own judgement to know when the model is wrong.

Industry observers note that build internal security tooling: contribute to the CVE registry and related automation that connects scanners, engineering teams, and customer communication. Much of it is built on Camunda itself.

Help engineers do the secure thing by default: answer questions, review pull requests, improve guidelines and occasionally run a session or workshop.

On-call and incident response: share the InfoSec on-call rotation with the other engineers and help investigate and resolve security incidents.

Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

What You Will Bring to the Role.

Around 3+ years in security or software engineering, with at least 2 of them working on application or product security (AppSec, product security, pentesting, or a security-focused developer role all count).

Experience at a SaaS or software product tech giant, working closely with engineering teams that ship often through modern CI/CD and cloud environments.

Hands-on vulnerability triage: you've worked with tools like Snyk, Trivy, Semgrep, CodeQL or similar, can tell a real issue from a false positive, and can explain how exploitable something actually is in context (CVSS, exploitability, configuration).

It has been revealed that threat modeling and design review experience (e.g. STRIDE) on real systems, ideally web apps, APIs, or distributed services.

In a recent development, you read and write code. You're comfortable reading Java (Camunda is built on it) well enough to follow a data flow and spot a security bug. You can write scripts and small tools and contribute to an existing codebase with review.

You build with AI, not just chat with it. You use AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot or similar) in your daily work to write tools, analyse code or automate tasks. And you know their output still needs a second look, especially when it comes to security.

Sources indicate that clear, friendly communication with engineers. You see yourself as an enabler, not a gatekeeper, and you can explain risk to people who aren't security specialists.

Some Python and/or JavaScript experience, or experience building internal tools.

Willingness to learn and use Camunda, since we build a lot of our own security automation on it. Prior BPMN / workflow experience is a plus.

Experience responding to security incidents or being part of an on-call rotation.

Exposure to security advisories, CVE disclosure or bug bounty programmes.

Knowledge of AI/LLM security risks (OWASP Top 10 for LLMs / agentic apps, prompt injection, tool abuse).

Experience securing Kubernetes or container-based workloads, or open-source / B2B software.

Sources indicate that right now, if you don’t want your site to be scraped by AI companies, you have to block each company’s crawlers individually. On Friday, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Microsoft said they would support a common robots.txt signal that, per OpenAI, “makes it easier for publishers and website operators to communicate the same preference to multiple participating providers at once.”.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic engineer Kevin Kelley proposed the common signal as part of work for the Internet Engineering Task Force, and Anthropic is already supporting it. OpenAI indicates it will do so “in the coming months,” and Google and Microsoft say they’ll do so next year.

Meta VP of communications Andy Stone called the common signal “an key step,” writing in a tweet that the company supports “publishers’ ability to express preferences about how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.” Meta is under scrutiny for proposed commercial terms that would allow broad scraping; last week, it agreed to delay implementation of those terms.

    Robots.txt Guide – Best Practices For Search & AI Crawlers via @sejournal, @vahandev

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The robots.txt file has always been an essential tool for managing crawler access to a website.
    • Sources indicate that but, blocking the wrong bot can exclude your content from LLMs or SERPs, while leaving unnecessary URLs open can waste crawl budget on large sites.
    • This guide will help you understand how robots.txt rules work so you can avoid common robots.txt mistakes, keep useful content accessible, but at the same time limit unnecessary crawling.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The robots.txt file has always been an essential tool for managing crawler access to a website. With AI search tools and agents now visiting websites alongside traditional crawlers, you need to know which rules each one follows.

    Sources indicate that but, blocking the wrong bot can exclude your content from LLMs or SERPs, while leaving unnecessary URLs open can waste crawl budget on large sites. So, you need to know what you are doing.

    This guide will help you understand how robots.txt rules work so you can avoid common robots.txt mistakes, keep useful content accessible, but at the same time limit unnecessary crawling.

    The robots.txt is a simple text file that sits in the root directory of your site and tells crawlers what should be crawled.

    The table below provides a quick reference to the key robots.txt directives.

    This 2024 screenshot indicates an example of robots.txt from ikea.com with multiple rules.

    Note that robots.txt doesn’t support full regular expressions and only has two wildcards:.

    Also, note that URL path matching is case-sensitive, e.g., “filter=” is not equal to “Filter=.” The directive names and user-agent matching are case-insensitive.

    When setting up a robots.txt file, it’s important to know the order in which search engines decide which rules to apply in case of conflicting rules.

    When you write a separate set of rules for a bot, it follows those rules instead of the rules under User-agent: *. For example:.

    Here, Googlebot can crawl /private/ because its own rules allow every URL to be crawled. To block that directory for Googlebot, add Disallow: /private/ beneath its Allow: / line.

    Within the applicable group, Google follows these two key rules:.

    The rule that matches more characters in the URL will be applied. For example:.

    In this case, the “Allow: /downloads/free/” rule is more specific than “Disallow: /downloads/” because it targets a subdirectory.

    Google will allow crawling of subfolder “/downloads/free/” but block everything else under “/downloads/.”.

    When multiple rules are equally specific, for example:.

    Google will choose the least restrictive one. This means Google will allow access to /downloads/.

    Google’s 2024 reminder about action URLs focused on add-to-cart and wishlist links that waste crawler and server resources.

    Recent findings suggest that imagine you have an online store with hundreds of thousands of pages. There are sections of websites like filtered pages that may have an infinite number of versions. Those pages don’t have unique value, essentially contain duplicate content, and may create infinite crawl space, thus wasting your server and Googlebot’s resources. That is where robots.txt comes in, preventing search engine bots from crawling those pages.

    If you don’t do that, Google may try to crawl an infinite number of URLs with different (even non-existent) search parameter values, causing spikes and a waste of crawl budget.

    As a general rule, you should always ask why certain pages exist, and whether they have any value for search engines to crawl and index.

    Depending on your site and indexing goals, candidates for crawl restrictions include:.

    Let’s dive into examples of how you can use robots.txt for each case.

    Internal search results are a common source of unnecessary crawling by Google and other search engines. If those results are not intended to appear in search, consider restricting their crawl space.

    On WordPress websites, it is usually an “s” parameter, and the URL looks like this:.

    Gary Illyes from Google has repeatedly warned to block “action” URLs as they can cause Googlebot to crawl them indefinitely even non-existent URLs with different combinations.

    Here is the rule you can use in your robots.txt to block such URLs from being crawled:.

    This crawl-stats screenshot, included in the original 2024 guide, illustrates reduced crawling of non-existent internal search URLs after they were blocked via robots.txt.

    Note that Google may index blocked pages based on links to their URLs. Robots.txt does not guarantee their removal from search. If removal is your goal, use noindex and allow Google to crawl the page so it can read that instruction.

    Industry observers note that faceted navigation is an integral part of every ecommerce website. There can be cases where faceted navigation is part of an SEO strategy and aimed at ranking for general product searches.

    Sources indicate that zalando’s color-based landing pages, such as those targeting “gray t-shirt” illustrate this approach. The principle is to keep useful search landing pages crawlable while restricting unwanted filter combinations.

    However, in most cases, this is not the case, and filter parameters are used merely for filtering products, creating dozens of pages with duplicate content.

    Recent findings suggest that there may be multiple filter parameters in one URL. Identify which ones generate unwanted crawl space; do not block facets that form part of your search strategy. Google’s faceted-navigation guidance distinguishes these two cases.

    For example, if you have filters with the following parameters “sortby,” “color,” and “price,” you may use this set of rules:.

    These pairs match each parameter in the first position or after another parameter. Add only the parameters you intend to restrict, and test both wanted and unwanted URLs.

    UTM parameters are used for tracking purposes.

    Recent findings suggest that in the Reddit exchange shown below, John Mueller addressed tracking parameters on external links. Keep that context separate from internally generated filter or search URLs.

    Keep internal links pointed at the URLs you want crawled. Decide whether to block a parameter by what it does on your site; the presence of a query string alone is not a reason to disallow a page.

    Let’s say you have a lot of PDF documents, such as product guides, brochures, or downloadable papers, and you don’t want them crawled.

    Here is a simple robots.txt rule that will block search engine bots from accessing those documents:.

    The “Disallow: /*.pdf$” line tells crawlers not to crawl any URLs that end with .pdf.

    By using /*, the rule matches any path on the website. As a result, any URL ending with .pdf will be blocked from crawling. It will not match /guide.pdf?download=1 or an uppercase .PDF extension; test any such variants separately. If you want a PDF excluded from search, use an X-Robots-Tag: noindex HTTP header and keep it crawlable so Google can read the header.

    If you have a WordPress website and want to disallow PDFs from the uploads directory where you upload them via the CMS, you can use the following rule:.

    You can see that we have conflicting rules here.

    In case of conflicting rules, the more specific one takes priority, which means the last line ensures that only the specific file located in folder “wp-content/uploads/2024/09/allowed-document.pdf” is allowed to be crawled.

    Recent findings suggest that let’s say you have an API endpoint where you submit your data from the form. It is likely your form has an action attribute like action=”/form/submissions/.”.

    If a crawler discovers the URL /form/submissions/, you may want to prevent crawling of that path. You can request that with this rule:.

    By specifying a directory in the Disallow rule, you are telling the crawlers to avoid crawling all pages under that directory, and you don’t need to use the (*) wildcard anymore, like “/form/*.”.

    Note that you must always specify relative paths and never absolute URLs, like “https://www.example.com/form/” for Disallow and Allow directives.

    Be cautious to avoid malformed rules. For example, using /form without a trailing slash will also match a page /form-design-examples/, which may be a page on your blog that you want to index.

    Read: 8 Common Robots.txt Issues And How To Fix Them.

    If you have an ecommerce website, you likely have directories that start with “/myaccount/,” such as “/myaccount/orders/” or “/myaccount/profile/.”.

    With the top page “/myaccount/” being a sign-in page that you want to be indexed and found by users in search, you may want to disallow the subpages from being crawled by Googlebot.

    You can use the Disallow rule in combination with the Allow rule to block everything under the “/myaccount/” directory (except the /myaccount/ page).

    And again, since Google uses the most specific rule, it will disallow everything under the /myaccount/ directory but allow only the /myaccount/ page to be crawled.

    Here’s another use case of combining the Disallow and Allow rules: in case you have your search under the /search/ directory and want it to be found and indexed but block actual search URLs:.

    Every website uses JavaScript, and many of these scripts are not related to the rendering of content, such as tracking scripts or those used for loading AdSense.

    Only block a script after confirming it is unnecessary for rendering the content and links you want indexed. Use URL Inspection to check the rendered page; blocking a shared bundle or a script with rendering dependencies can prevent Google from seeing vital content. A robots.txt file on your host also cannot control a script fetched from a different host.

    Below is a sample line that is disallowing sample JavaScript, which contains tracking pixels.

    You can block training bots while allowing AI tools to find your pages and retrieve them for people. The key is to give training, search, and user-requested AI crawlers separate rules.

    Publishers may block training to limit the use of their reporting without attribution, while ecommerce brands may welcome it if product mentions lead people to search and buy. Because the benefits differ by business, developers should set these rules with stakeholders.

    Disallowing training bots cannot guarantee that your content stays out of training datasets, because crawlers that ignore robots.txt can still collect it. It also does not force AI tools to visit or cite your site, as they may find the information elsewhere.

    Recent findings suggest that A BuzzStream study covered by SEJ in January 2026, found that 79% of the US and UK news sites examined disallowed at least one training bot, while 71% disallowed at least one retrieval or live-search bot. Because retrieval helps AI tools find and cite your pages, blocking those bots is a separate decision from opting out of training.

    OpenAI uses OAI-SearchBot to surface websites in ChatGPT search answers, while ChatGPT-User handles user-requested visits. Because search and training permissions are separate, you can allow OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User while blocking GPTBot.

    This example blocks OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s training crawlers while allowing their search and user-requested bots, along with Perplexity’s:.

    It has been revealed that in the example above, /private/ is an excluded directory. Replace it with any paths you want to keep those bots from crawling.

    Most major AI crawlers follow robots.txt, including OpenAI’s GPTBot and Anthropic’s ClaudeBot.

    Industry observers note that user-requested visits work differently because some providers allow their bots to bypass robots.txt or generally ignore it when acting on a user’s request. OpenAI states robots.txt may not apply to ChatGPT-User, and Perplexity says Perplexity-User generally ignores it. Anthropic says its bots, including Claude-User, honor robots.txt. Because robots.txt only tells bots which URLs they may crawl, you need authentication to protect private content.

    The bot tokens and robots.txt policies for Copilot’s browser visits, Grok, DeepSeek, and Meta Muse remain unknown because I could not verify them in the providers’ public documentation.

    Google and Apple provide separate robots.txt tokens for controlling how crawled content is used:.

    Sources indicate that google-Extended covers Gemini training and specified grounding uses, where source content helps generate an answer. Blocking it does not block Googlebot or affect ordinary Google Search inclusion. Applebot-Extended controls foundation-model training without blocking Applebot’s search crawl. Neither token is a separate crawler, so these rules do not reduce crawling requests by themselves.

    After changing the file, check your server log files and confirm that your firewall allows the bots you want. Use server or CDN controls when you need to enforce access restrictions.

    For background, see SEJ’s earlier coverage of AI content use and AI chatbot traffic.

    In a recent development, including your sitemap URL in the robots.txt file helps search engines easily discover all the key pages on your website. This is done by adding a specific line that points to your sitemap location, and you can specify multiple sitemaps, each on its own line.

    Unlike Allow or Disallow rules, which allow only a relative path, the Sitemap directive requires a full, absolute URL to indicate the location of the sitemap.

    Ensure the sitemaps’ URLs are accessible to search engines and have proper syntax to avoid errors.

    It has been revealed that the crawl-delay directive in robots.txt specifies the number of seconds a bot should wait before crawling the next page. While Googlebot does not recognize the crawl-delay directive, other bots may respect it.

    It helps prevent server overload by controlling how frequently bots crawl your site.

    For example, if you want ClaudeBot to crawl your content for AI training but want to avoid server overload, you can set a crawl delay to manage the interval between requests.

    Industry observers note that this requests a 60-second delay from ClaudeBot, which Anthropic documents as supporting the non-standard Crawl-delay extension. Use this when you intend to allow that crawl. Adding a delay does not override a Disallow: / rule for the same bot; review the complete group rather than copying both policies.

    Of course, there may be AI bots that don’t respect crawl delay directives. In that case, you may need to use a web firewall to rate limit them.

    Once you’ve composed your robots.txt, you can use these tools to troubleshoot if the syntax is correct or if you didn’t accidentally block an important URL.

    Once you’ve updated your robots.txt, you must check whether it contains any error or accidentally blocks URLs you want to be crawled, such as resources, images, or website sections.

    In a recent development, navigate to Settings > robots.txt to open the robots.txt report. It highlights the files Google fetched and any parsing warnings or errors. You can request a recrawl after a critical change. To test whether an individual page is blocked, use URL Inspection.

    The video below illustrates the report workflow; interface details may differ from the current version.

    Google’s robots.txt parser is an open-source parser and matcher based on the implementation used in Google’s crawler.

    Industry observers note that it requires advanced skills to install and run on your local computer. But it is highly recommended to take time and do it as instructed on that page because you can validate your changes in the robots.txt file before uploading to your server in line with the official Google parser.

    In a recent development, robots.txt rules apply to the host, protocol, and port where the file is requested. If you need crawl restrictions on a subdomain, its robots.txt URL must serve the rules or redirect to a file that does; the parent domain’s file is not inherited.

    It creates challenges when you have a website with a dozen subdomains, as it means you should maintain a bunch of robots.txt files separately.

    However, it is possible to host a robots.txt file on a subdomain, such as https://cdn.example.com/robots.txt, and set up a redirect from https://www.example.com/robots.txt to it.

    You can do vice versa and host it only under the root domain and redirect from subdomains to the root.

    Sources indicate that google applies the retrieved rules to the host that originally requested robots.txt, not automatically to the host storing the shared file. Configure a redirect from each host you want to manage, and check that the shared paths make sense for all of them.

    It has been revealed that it helps make updates and maintenance more efficient. Otherwise, you would need to use a separate robots.txt file for each subdomain.

    A properly optimized robots.txt file is crucial for managing a website’s crawl budget. It ensures that search engines like Googlebot spend their time on valuable pages rather than wasting resources on unnecessary ones.

    It has been revealed that blocking compliant crawlers can reduce unwanted requests. For AI systems, distinguish crawl restrictions from training-use controls, and verify the effect in your logs. Google-Extended and Applebot-Extended do not stop a separate crawler.

    Make sure you always validate your changes to avoid unexpected crawlability complications.

    It has been revealed that however, remember that crawl demand and serving capacity both matter. Useful content, efficient page loading, and a healthy server remain notable alongside robots.txt rules.

    All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”.

    Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

    Sources indicate that but not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

    According to recent reports, “Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres stated. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”.

    Industry observers note that mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

    Industry observers note that to reach newly introduced audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Industry observers note that from the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

    Recent findings suggest that “The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is right now a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

    A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay).

    Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for substantial investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”.

    It has been revealed that not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

    “People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres stated. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”.

    CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

    It has been revealed that “We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”.

    Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

    RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”.

    It has been revealed that looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.).

    Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler noted. Only 21% were “doom only.”.

    According to recent reports, the video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

    “We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres noted. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”.

    What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.).

    “I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler noted. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”.

    It has been revealed that part of the problem, he remarked, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”.

    #43952. OpenAI Publishes Prompting Guidance For GPT-6.2 Astra via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (919 w)

    OpenAI Publishes Prompting Guidance For GPT-6.2 Astra via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, openAI is suggesting that developers who are migrating to GPT-6.2 Astra should revisit instructions such as “be concise” when they patch their system prompts.
    • The organization’s guidance for GPT-6 Astra notes the model tends toward detailed, formatted responses.
    • GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol introduced Nov.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, openAI is suggesting that developers who are migrating to GPT-6.2 Astra should revisit instructions such as “be concise” when they patch their system prompts. The guide for developers on how to use GPT-6.2 states that Astra produces output that is more direct and brief by default than prior GPT models.

    The organization’s guidance for GPT-6 Astra notes the model tends toward detailed, formatted responses.

    GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol introduced Nov. 17. Developers can use both in the API as gpt-6.2-astra and gpt-6.2-sol.

    Astra is described in the GPT-6.2 guide as “more concise and direct by default than earlier models,” with an adjustable overall tone that can range from a professional colleague to a more conversational assistant.

    The GPT-6.2 guide provides an example prompt for apps that use the model as a collaborator in day-to-day work. This prompt tells Astra to stick with the terminology of the user and its sources and to address the key points at the outset of its response.

    The GPT-6 guidance states, “GPT-6 Astra tends to use lists, tables and Markdown to make responses scannable.” The GPT-6 guide also contains an example prompt for apps that require prose with less formatting. This example prompt requests “clear, concise paragraphs” and directs the model to reserve lists for presenting parallel or sequential data.

    The GPT-5.6 guide states that GPT-5.6 is generally more concise by default than GPT-5.5, and that brevity instructions (such as “Be concise” and “Keep it short”) may be unnecessary for some types of task.

    Industry observers note that the GPT-6.2 guide advises asking the model to adjust for its target audience in emails, documents and any other writing intended for an external reader. It does this by suggesting a prompt which states that an external audience would probably have less understanding of the user’s context, so the model will need to provide the background information that audience needs.

    The prompt also provides guidance on editing by instructing the model to “preserve the author’s content and wording” when reviewing or editing existing work and adhere to the user’s direction as to what changes are to be made.

    In a recent development, when performing longer tasks, the model can retain abbreviations, jargon or shorthand from the reasoning process, or from other agents, in its final answers. The guide suggests a method to address this by having the model write a self-contained response for anyone who hasn’t been tracking progress updates. Additionally, the guide’s example prompt tells the model not to include such shorthand, jargon or abbreviations in the response.

    Sources indicate that the guide says GPT-6.2 Astra may propose a next step and wait for confirmation when a user’s intent is unclear. For work that can run on its own, the guide’s advice is to spell out the outcome the model should complete and which decisions need the user’s input.

    The guide’s suggested prompts tell the model to make reasonable, reversible assumptions and keep working, stating what it assumed. It should stop and ask only when the task’s scope changes in a major way, when it’s blocked, or when the user has to make a decision. It should also check in before irreversible or destructive actions.

    Sources indicate that the guide also points to an async question tool, which lets GPT-6.2 ask the user a question while it keeps working on anything that doesn’t depend on the answer. OpenAI’s async tool calling page says the app defines that tool and shows the question to the user, and that it isn’t a built-in tool in the Responses API.

    According to recent reports, starting with GPT-6.2, the API will drop reasoning items as soon as it identifies that the client has made an edit to prior history, dropped down to a lower model version, or changed the end-user account or organization, according to OpenAI’s API documentation. Reasoning items provide the model’s reasoning from earlier in the conversation. Dropping these can lead to a reduction in answer quality and increase the number of tokens used by the model to repeat previous work.

    Sources indicate that examples on OpenAI’s page about the change include shortening a tool result, rewriting a developer message (which carries an app’s instructions), and replacing older turns with a summary. For new instructions, the page suggests appending a developer message that asks the model to ignore older instructions and follow the new ones, in place of editing the original.

    Sources indicate that teams building drafting or editing tools on GPT-6 Astra have prompts to review prior to migrating to GPT-6.2 Astra. Developers need to revisit any instruction that asks GPT-6 Astra to produce briefer answers, according to the 6.2 guide. Some of these tools may rewrite their own instructions as well during a conversation. This could lead to GPT-6.2 Astra losing its earlier reasoning, and spending additional tokens to recreate this process.

    Recent findings suggest that the GPT-6.2 guide calls its prompts a starting point, based on behavior seen with GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. The GPT-6 guidance is still on the same page as the 6.2 guide, under its own tab, so teams can compare what each guide indicates about the model they’re moving from.

    For reasoning effort, the 6.2 migration notes recommend medium for new integrations and low for apps that are at the moment set to none or minimal. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 guide, which I covered in September, also asked developers to retest effort settings carried over from Opus 5.
