    At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    Atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured American to get life-changing aid. Our mission is to tear down barriers between people in crisis and the aid they deserve. In the last six years, we’ve become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We also help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    So far, we’ve helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10 billion in life-changing aid —and earned over 20,000 five-star reviews. And we’re just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, Google Ventures, and True Ventures, and we’re on our way to creating a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    In a recent development, each day, thousands of people seek our help getting disability benefits or insurance compensation. They’re intimidated by the process, unsure where to turn, and desperate for good advice.

    As a Legal Assistant at Atticus, your job is to ensure they get and stay on the right path. This job is different from that of a traditional legal assistant. The job mixes responsibilities in any good legal assistant’s comfort zone (build client relationships; support paralegals and attorneys in filing and managing claims) with those unique to being an operator in a fast-growing tech tech giant (help Marketing source clients who’d be great in testimonials, or user test latest tools for Product).

    In a typical week you might do any of the following:.

    Make contact with a client that’s in danger of slipping through the cracks at SSA, and help get their case back on track.

    Work with a client’s team to run down missing paperwork at SSA.

    Take on an inefficient workflow that’s slowing the team down (e.g., processing case updates), scope an improvement, get team buy-in, and execute the improvement.

    According to recent reports, this role is a rare opportunity to join a fast-growing Series C startup and do meaningful social impact work. It’s designed to be a path to building expertise in the fields of law you support and taking on greater responsibilities over time (e.g. becoming a paralegal).

    You have a Bachelor’s degree from a four-year university with strong academic performance.

    You have experience in a professional role that required a substantial amount of customer-facing work and/or administrative tasks.

    You are a resourceful team-player ready to dive into a scrappy startup environment where you will learn promptly and get your hands dirty.

    You are comfortable in a variety of interpersonal conversations; you can be empathetic and kind when speaking with people in a moment of crisis, and can be thoughtful and organized when interacting with attorneys or the SSA.

    You have a demonstrated commitment to doing good and helping people.

    You have professional experience helping others apply for government benefits.

    You have experience at a startup or other fast-paced, agile environment.

    According to recent reports, we are strongly committed to building a diverse team. If you’re from a background that’s underrepresented in tech, we’d love to meet you.

    This is a rare opportunity to join a startup that has strong traction (substantial funding, well-respected backers, tremendous growth, and many happy customers) but is still small enough that you can have a huge impact and play a role in shaping our culture.

    It has been revealed that we’re a certified B Corporation tackling a critical social problem. Our mission to help people in need drives everything we do, and your work here will touch many lives.

    We offer competitive pay — including equity for every employee — and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employees and their families premiums covered.

    15 vacation days & ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at the end-of-year).

    $1,000/year reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    We anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $50,000 and $75,000 in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as candidate’s experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    This job is fully remote and we’re committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the firm dime) as needed to be with your colleagues – usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • Industry observers note that we will never sell your address.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    Industry observers note that we will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    Stations in Upcoming Hampshire, Wisconsin, Massachusetts, and Utah all climbed in our regular ranking of public radio stations between July and September.

    According to recent reports, more than a year ago, NHPR reporter Todd Bookman started asking questions about “an irregular personnel maneuver” involving the chief justice of Latest Hampshire’s Supreme Court. Bookman’s reporting ultimately became “Exhibit A” in the ethics probe that led to the justice’s resignation in September.

    In a recent development, the bombshell resignation news was NHPR’s biggest story in September — and of 2026 to date. The story helped push NHPR up several spots in our regular ranking of public radio websites. NHPR saw visits rise 22% that month, according to Similarweb visit figures compiled by Nieman Lab.

    RELATED ARTICLECollaborations and primary elections boosted traffic to public media sites this quarterNeel DhaneshaJuly 29, 2026At the very top of the list, not much moved. The Chicago Sun-Times, owned by Chicago Public Media, held onto the top spot, followed by Gothamist (from WNYC) and Minnesota Public Radio. As Nieman Lab senior writer Joshua Benton wrote when introducing the rankings, which we’ve also done for local newspapers and local nonprofit news sites, not all markets are created equal. Public radio stations serving major metropolitan areas with lots of college graduates have a bigger potential audience than stations serving smaller communities and areas with fewer resources. And, of course, Similarweb provides an estimate; internal metrics may differ. Still, the rankings are a valuable window into some industry-wide trends, and often an opportunity to highlight local news organizations punching above their weight.

    According to recent reports, like several public media sites on our list, election season provided a bump to NHPR. New Hampshire held its primary on Sept. 8 and the statewide public radio station saw a traffic boost from results pages and campaign coverage, remarked NHPR director of audience engagement Casey McDermott. She described September as a solid month, not an outlier. “But what makes September an exceptionally cool case study is that it reflects two fundamentals at the heart of our mission: a commitment to fresh, local reporting and a renewed internal investment in digital publishing,” McDermott said. “[Bookman’s piece] wasn’t just a standard breaking news item — it was the culmination of months of meticulous accountability reporting,” McDermott added. On the audience side, McDermott said that, in addition to a boost from NHPR’s partners at NPR and Google News, the chief justice story benefited from X (formerly known as Twitter). A post by NHPR president and CEO Jim Schachter caught on and inspired “a stream of supportive comments about the importance of local journalism.” BREAKING: Fearless reporting by New Hampshire Public Radio results in the resignation of the chief justice of the New Hampshire Supreme Court. #NHPolitics https://t.co/6DtIeEIwdp — Jim Schachter (@jimschachter) September 15, 2026 WBUR, one of two Boston-based public media stations, grew every month this quarter, moving from 1.45 million visits to 2.1 million in September, according to Similarweb. WBUR had the biggest raw gain of any station in September. Tiffany Campbell, WBUR’s executive editor for digital audience and news, said organic search traffic and Google Discover helped. “We’ve been working on building out many referral streams,” Campbell said, “but in early September Google delivered a lot of organic search audience via a couple of strong stories.” “Our referral diversification aims to be less reliant on Google organic search but it’s also crucial to take advantage when it delivers,” she added. Those strong stories? An explainer on the insanity defense during jury deliberations in Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial, results from the Massachusetts primary held on Sept. 1, and a Here & Now interview with Associated Press photographer Richard Drew — who took the “Falling Man” photo — on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. All three stories drew both local and national readers, Campbell said. Campbell credited the steady rise in traffic to “things we’re always doing: in-depth local coverage, comprehensive reporting on a closely watched election (which was an early indication of interest in the general election in November) and relevant enterprise reporting.” The Milwaukee-based WUWM was the fastest climber in the top 25 this quarter. The station nearly doubled its visits between June and September, rising in our ranking from No. 31 to No. 15. According to Similarweb, the station’s visits rose 32% in August and by another 17% in September. Michelle Maternowski, WUWM audience innovation manager, said the surge started with Wisconsin’s August 11 primary. “We published our Voter Guide in time for that and saw a decent amount come to our meet the candidate posts,” she said. Readers were especially interested in news and information on the lesser-known races. “We see lots of traffic to the down ballot, statewide races — like state treasurer and secretary of state.” And then there’s the gift that keeps on giving. Published in 2019, WUWM’s segment on the 150th birthday of the periodic table still ranks “really high in search results.” “I think once the school year started up again, a lot of students were searching their periodic tables,” Maternowski said. “It is very silly that this story continues to get so much traffic.” If you only look at the top 25 stations, you’ll miss some impressive jumps. The Salt Lake City-based KUER, for example, took the biggest leap in ranking of any station in July. The station’s visits rose 122% that month, according to Similarweb’s numbers. “The numbers don’t lie,” Jim Hill, digital manager in the KUER newsroom, confirmed. “July was a monster for us.” Hill had expected a “plateau or small retreat” after a record year in 2025 — which included the Charlie Kirk killing and a shooting at a No Kings Protest in Utah. Instead, the news site has been ahead of last year’s pace. Total customers are up 19% over last year, even after attempts to filter out bots, and social media referrals falling by 54%. (Hill noted the station’s social media producer was laid off and that KUER is attempting to “pivot to video/reels.”) The station saw “some runaway Google Discover success” last year but, in 2026, clicks from Google Discover are “less than half” of its 2025 figures. Hill credited “engagement reporting and audience-valued topics” that have “kept audiences reading” despite the headwinds. KUER also grew its “owned” email audience and drove 34% more users to the website compared to 2025, according to Hill. All in all, July was “very hit-heavy,” Hill said. The top 10 stories — led by Donald Trump’s decision to dramatically shrink two Utah national monuments — accounted for 64% of the month’s views. The station also saw a major boost from NPR, including multiple stories from a week-long hearing in the Charlie Kirk case. “Our newsroom was the ground team for NPR, so the network highlighted web coverage nationally,” Hill said. Most of the audience came from outside Utah. Hill said NPR can be directly attributed for 32% of sessions, Google Search 14%, and Google News 13.5%. Two wildfire stories also gave major traffic boosts. But audiences especially loved hearing about Utah getting full-color specialty license plates. The story was KUER’s top Google Discover story in July and also got a significant bump (14% of visits) from Reddit. “We affectionately refer to stories like this as license plate news,” Hill said. “It always hits with the audience.” Sure enough, a second plate story, on Utah cracking down on the infamous “Montana loophole,” ended the month as the No. 2 Discover story.     From YouTube views to crypto hacks, subscription cyclones to Czech hats: Have you kept up with this week’s media news?

    It’s been yet another busy week. Recap it with the fourth edition of the Nieman Lab News-About-News Quiz, your weekly incentive to keep up with the latest happenings in the world of digital journalism. All questions are based on the week’s Nieman Lab stories or articles elsewhere that we’ve linked to in What We’re Reading. This is the final edition of the quiz for 2026; if people seem to like it, we’ll keep it going in 2027. Good luck!

    According to recent reports, the Chicago Sun-Times unveiled a new slogan this week. What is it?

    “Chicago’s Paper” replaces “The Hardest-Working Paper in America,” the paper’s slogan since 2018.

    An “overwhelming majority” of American journalists employed by this tech giant voted this week to authorize a strike.

    “The union has been negotiating a new contract for more than a year, and leaders say disagreements over wages, artificial intelligence and manager overreach have forced them to take this step.”.

    Recent findings suggest that A “digital experience platform” company whose software runs on many news sites was hacked this week, sending malware to readers of the BBC, CNN, and Fox News. What’s the company’s name?

    The hack stole cryptocurrency and credit card numbers from an unknown number of news site visitors.

    Recent findings suggest that A major journalism school announced this week that its master’s degree programs would now be tuition-free for in-state residents. Which school?

    “Newmark J-School’s campaign for free tuition is rooted in CUNY’s decades-long commitment to access and opportunity for Latest Yorkers. At a time of profound transformation in the news industry, removing the cost of tuition makes it easier for more people to take the risk of entering the field.”.

    At this week’s summit in China, Bloomberg TV reporter Annmarie Hordern asked Donald Trump whether he felt Nvidia founder Jensen Huang had been disloyal to the United States. What happened next?

    “It was the latest example of China’s strict controls on news coverage and how tightly Beijing tries to stage-manage major international events.”.

    Paid digital subscriptions at McClatchy-owned publications — a group that includes the Miami Herald, the Kansas City Star, and the Charlotte Observer — have declined how much in the past year, according to an internal corporate presentation?

    Sources indicate that unique visitors have also dropped by 39%. McClatchy’s response? Doubling down on AI.

    This is the per capita annual funding for public media across a set of five rich countries: $110, $81, $53, $27, $3. Name the five countries, in order.

    With prospects for public media brighter with a Democratic Congress, some advocates are calling for a big increase in the United States’ historically puny funding levels.

    YouTube has found a latest way to inflate the number of “views” a video on its platform gets. What is it?

    “YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also claims the change will help it align with ‘TV industry standards,’ which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows.”.

    It has been revealed that in Czechia, mass rallies in support of public broadcasting have featured protestors wearing a very specific hat. Whose hat is it?

    Since 1965, Večerníček (a diminutive of večerník, meaning evening newspaper) has appeared on Czech Television every night at 6:45 p.m. to wish children goodnight. Demonstrators wore his hat during the country’s largest protests since 1989 to oppose government plans to scrap public media license fees.

    Salesforce CEO Says ‘Goodbye SEO.’ Salesforce’s SEO Guide Disagrees via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (513 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, on Nov.
    • Benioff wrote in his post that customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead are asking Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants which brands they should purchase.
    • Several SEO professionals countered Benioff’s claims in quote posts and replies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, on Nov. 18, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff mentioned “Goodbye SEO” on X, promoting Palmata, an AI-based tool for tracking how visible a manufacturer is in AI answers, while a Salesforce guide linked on Palmata’s page states SEO “is still the foundation.”.

    Benioff wrote in his post that customers “aren’t searching anymore” but instead are asking Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and other AI assistants which brands they should purchase. The post further states, “No click. No referral. Nothing in your analytics,” and then pitches Palmata as a tool that monitors what AI assistants say about a business, offers recommendations on what changes need to be made, and simulates the effect of those changes prior to publication.

    Several SEO professionals countered Benioff’s claims in quote posts and replies.

    Salesforce’s guide to SEO and AEO (answer engine optimization) states SEO “isn’t going away” and that “SEO is still the foundation.” Graham Hardt, whose byline lists him as SEO Senior Director, wrote it for fresh businesses, and Salesforce published it Sept. 11. Palmata’s product page links to the guide from its FAQ.

    Industry observers note that contentful introduced Palmata in June; it became a part of Salesforce when Salesforce’s acquisition of Contentful occurred on Sept. 1. The article announcing the launch of Palmata, written by Jason McGhee, head of product and engineering for Palmata, remarked that SEO gave organizations “a practical framework for improving visibility” and added, “That work remains essential.”.

    Aleyda Solis, an SEO and AI search consultant who founded Orainti, wrote in a quote post that AI search “relies on many of the same fundamentals as SEO.” Her post continues, “AI search optimization goes beyond traditional SEO, but it certainly doesn’t replace it.”.

    Solis also wrote that measuring AI search visibility matters, “but monitoring what AI platforms say about your brand and actually improving your visibility, recommendations and business outcomes are very different things.”.

    Pedro Dias, a technical SEO product manager who used to work at Google, wrote that SEO “was never a topic that attracted the interest of decision makers.” His post adds, “SEO isn’t traffic. It never has been.”.

    Lily Ray, who founded Algorythmic, replied to Benioff, “This gold rush already happened and the market is already oversaturated.” Growth advisor Eli Schwartz wrote that “there’s yet another AEO tool in the mix.”.

    When Benioff’s post is read by a marketing executive, Salesforce’s own guide answers it, stating that SEO and AEO are “two visibility layers for the same audience.”.

    In terms of making the case for upcoming businesses to include both SEO and AEO, this guide provides Salesforce’s reasoning for including SEO in your looks right alongside any AI visibility tool, such as Palmata.

    In a recent development, according to Palmata’s FAQ section, Palmata is a standalone tool that is also built into Marketing Cloud by Salesforce. In weighing tools like Palmata, Salesforce’s guide states you should track “both sets of metrics.” This means tracking your organic traffic and rankings, but also tracking how many times you’ve been cited by AI.

    Public Policy Lead - UK at Kindred

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Kindred is a members-only home swapping platform that unlocks the ability to live a travel-rich lifestyle through the power of community.
    • Kindred is revolutionizing the “third option” of travel accommodation, compared to short-term rentals and hotels.
    • To support that momentum, Kindred has raised over $150M in capital from some of the most credible investors in Silicon Valley, including Index Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, New Enterprise Associates, Bessemer Venture Partners, Caffeinated Capital, Elad Gil, and founders of companies like Opendoor, Figma, ClassPass, and more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kindred is a members-only home swapping platform that unlocks the ability to live a travel-rich lifestyle through the power of community. By exchanging primary residences with trusted peers, renters and owners alike can match with Kindred spirits and explore new destinations without breaking the bank.

    Kindred is revolutionizing the “third option” of travel accommodation, compared to short-term rentals and hotels. Since launching in 2022, Kindred has grown to a global community of 300,000 members across 150+ cities and puts home swapping on the map as a radically more affordable, responsible, and connected way to travel.

    To support that momentum, Kindred has raised over $150M in capital from some of the most credible investors in Silicon Valley, including Index Ventures, Andreessen Horowitz, New Enterprise Associates, Bessemer Venture Partners, Caffeinated Capital, Elad Gil, and founders of companies like Opendoor, Figma, ClassPass, and more.

    Kindred’s co-founders are proven leaders from the early team at Opendoor ($15B+ exit), who have each built and scaled products that today generate $1B+ annual revenue combined.

    We’re looking for the world’s top builders, executors, and believers to help us make travel more meaningful.

    You can learn more about us in Forbes and The New York Times.

    This is Kindred’s first dedicated public policy hire. You’ll join a three-person legal and policy team (reporting to the General Counsel) and own the execution of Kindred’s public policy and government relations efforts, with a focus on European markets but covering additional markets as necessary.

    The role is primarily focused on proactive advocacy to shape the policy environment for home-swapping. You’ll build relationships with elected officials, regulators, and industry groups. You’ll commission and manage economic impact research. You’ll develop city-level partnerships that normalize home-swapping as a category distinct from other travel categories. You’ll also develop working familiarity with the tax, housing, and accommodation regulations that intersect with Kindred’s model, and help parse how those frameworks apply (or don’t) to credit-based home-swapping. You’ll do all of this initially as a team of one, with outside consultants to support you and a path to building a team as the tech giant grows and the function matures.

    Execute Kindred’s public policy strategy with an emphasis on proactive advocacy.

    Industry observers note that build and maintain relationships with elected officials, regulators, and staff at the local, state/provincial, and national levels. Represent Kindred in meetings, hearings, coalition convenings, and industry events.

    Track proposed housing, short-term rental, tax, and platform regulations that could impact Kindred’s model, identifying where Kindred’s credit-based, non-commercial structure creates meaningful regulatory distinctions. Use AI-assisted tools and other technology to monitor developments across jurisdictions.

    In a recent development, further develop and evolve Kindred’s core policy narrative and positioning materials. Draft position papers, comment letters, testimony, and advocacy materials.

    In a recent development, propose and negotiate city-level partnerships that promote and normalize home-swapping. Build relationships with housing advocacy organizations, tourism boards, trade associations, and aligned industry coalitions.

    Commission and manage third-party economic analyses on the impact of Kindred’s model, collaborating with internal business teams and outside consulting firms.

    Identify, evaluate, and manage outside consultants cost-effectively (lobbyists, policy advisors, research firms).

    Partner with internal teams to develop externally facing materials and data packages for stakeholder engagements.

    Coordinate with the General Counsel on lobbying compliance, political activity disclosures, and regulatory filings.

    7–10 years of experience in public policy, with at least 3 years at a technology company or similar fast paced environment.

    Experience building or meaningfully contributing to building a public policy or government relations function, not just operating within an established one.

    Track record of productive relationships with elected officials, regulators, and policy stakeholders.

    Experience managing outside consultants, lobbyists, or policy advisors across multiple jurisdictions.

    Strong written and verbal communication skills, including experience drafting policy position papers, advocacy materials, or regulatory comments.

    Experience with policy matters in Europe, with an interest in policy work in fresh jurisdictions.

    Fluency with AI tools and a willingness to integrate them into policy monitoring, research, and content development workflows.

    Willingness to operate as an individual contributor while building the function, with the judgment to know when to engage outside support.

    Experience in or adjacent to the sharing economy, home-sharing, travel, housing, or short-term rental sectors.

    Experience at a growth-stage tech giant (under 500 employees).

    Familiarity with vacation/short-term rental, housing, and land use regulations, as well as related tax regulations.

    Comfort with detailed regulatory analysis: ability to read and interpret statutes, ordinances, and administrative rules, and translate their implications into actionable policy positions. A law degree and legal practice experience is a plus but not required.

    Build something fresh: You’ll help define the function and shape how Kindred engages with governments and regulators from the ground up.

    A genuinely different model: Kindred’s credit-based, non-commercial home-swapping model is structurally distinct from existing travel lodging categories, contributing to sustainable tourism objectives.

    Path to leadership: As the company and function grow, this role offers the opportunity to greater leadership.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates include a WordPress default that you will need to decide on, newly introduced data from Search Console via the API, and the question of which party determines whether Googlebot, AI agents or Google’s own calls will be allowed through.
    • According to recent reports, wordPress 7.2 will introduce a /random/ redirect (turned on by default), and Google has added branded data to the Search Console API.
    • Recent findings suggest that wordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to the week’s Pulse: updates include a WordPress default that you will need to decide on, newly introduced data from Search Console via the API, and the question of which party determines whether Googlebot, AI agents or Google’s own calls will be allowed through.

    According to recent reports, wordPress 7.2 will introduce a /random/ redirect (turned on by default), and Google has added branded data to the Search Console API. Google also published the referrer values its traffic sends and shared ways in which a CDN move could lead to blocking Googlebot. Ask Maps began contacting local businesses, and United Airlines included its AI agent rules within its terms.

    Here’s what matters for you and your work.

    Recent findings suggest that wordPress version 7.2, which is scheduled for Dec. 8, contains a new feature called /random/, turned on by default, to send a visitor to a randomly selected published post. There is no option in the dashboard settings for this to be turned off.

    It has been revealed that key facts: According to the developer note, /random/ randomly selects posts and also custom post types as long as they are publicly queryable and have archives (unless the developer has registered them using 'randomable' => false) and excludes pages and attachments. The development code uses a 302 status code along with an X-Robots-Tag: noindex, follow HTTP header when it redirects the visitor but does not send that header on the post that the visitor arrives at. To turn the feature off, developers need the wp_enable_random_content_redirect filter, and the different spelling given in WordPress’s November developer news roundup isn’t found anywhere in the code.

    Testimonials for clients (and other custom post type entries) may never be accessed via navigation. When their post type is eligible, they can be reached through /random/, even if they have been set to noindex by an SEO plugin. Before you upgrade, check which post types would meet WordPress’s eligibility criteria, and ask a developer to exclude those that should not show up.

    Industry observers note that read our full coverage: WordPress 7.2 Arrives Dec. 8 – Last-Minute Changes Still Being Made.

    Teams using the Search Console API can now segment the data they pull into branded and non-branded searches without having to maintain a list of their brands as regular expressions (regex).

    Sources indicate that key facts: Three Performance report features were added to the Search Analytics API by Google on Nov. 16. The brandedClassification dimension works only with eligible properties, and according to the API reference, the data provided for this dimension starts on Feb. 21, 2026. Setting type to webMultimodal returns results from Google Lens, Circle to Search on Android and image uploads, and a new filterLists field allows you to filter by multiple countries or devices in a single request.

    For reports covering dates before Feb. 21, 2026, you’ll still need your own brand regex. Google’s announcement of the branded queries filter claims “some queries may occasionally be misidentified,” so comparing the API split with the regex you already use can help you spot where they differ.

    Read our full coverage: Branded Query Data Is Now In The Google Search Console API.

    A google.com referrer lets you know in your analytics when Google sends a visitor, but it doesn’t show which source (Search, Discover or Google Images) was behind it, says a new Search Central page.

    Key facts: The page was listed Nov. 12 in Google’s documentation updates log. It says Google Search utilizes an origin referrer policy for its Search results; thus, the header will contain only the scheme and host, and not the search query. Referrers from Discover carry the values of the surface where Discover was viewed. Same-origin services such as Google Images send the same values as Search and Discover.

    Sources indicate that to distinguish Discover clicks from Search clicks, use Search Console’s Discover report rather than referrer data. If Google traffic appears as referral or direct in your analytics, Google’s page recommends checking whether custom channel rules, referral exclusions, or filters are reclassifying it.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Find Search Traffic In Analytics & Logs.

    A CDN can let Googlebot crawl your site faster before the CDN’s cache has filled, according to Google, and those requests then go to your origin server.

    Key facts: On Nov. 11, Search Central posted Google’s explanation that a fast and reliable CDN may slowly increase a site’s crawl capacity limit, while a brand new CDN begins with an empty cache. The first visit to each URL is a cache miss, so the page has to come from your origin server, and crawlers visit far more of your site’s URLs than visitors do, with most visitors sticking to a small set of popular pages. When admins block all bots from their site using blanket bot protection, they can cause Googlebot to fail CAPTCHA challenges. If this stays in place, then the pages of the site begin to drop out of search results.

    In a recent development, google’s advice for the move is to allow verified bots in the CDN and firewall settings, then pre-warm caches by fetching your most popular and frequently crawled URLs before switching traffic. Before enabling bot protection during the migration, be sure the verified-bot setting is turned on.

    Read our full coverage: Google Explains How To Avoid CDN Migration SEO Problems.

    Industry observers note that google’s Ask Maps has started calling some U.S. beauty, pet care, auto and home-repair businesses to identify available appointment times for customers.

    It has been revealed that key facts: On Nov. 16 a post from Google mentioned that customers can use Ask Maps to find these appointments online and have it call local businesses, then see available time slots so the customer can decide where to book. The feature started rolling out on Android and iOS, with the ability to find appointments launching in the U.S. first. Google already makes automated calls to businesses for customers using Google Search and Maps, including booking appointments and confirming availability, and this process is covered in Google’s Business Profile help page.

    In Google’s demo, Ask Maps indicates four times for a gel manicure that it confirmed were available online.

    Industry observers note that the setting Google documents for those automated calls is the “Bookings and inquiries from customers” option in Advanced settings in your verified Business Profile. However, Google’s Ask Maps post does not indicate if calls received via Ask Maps are subject to this setting. Check what you have set, and make sure whoever answers the phone knows these calls come from Google on behalf of a customer.

    Read our full coverage: Google Adds Appointment Finding & Business Calls To Ask Maps.

    United Airlines’ website terms, updated Nov. 11, let search engines index its public pages but require written permission for any AI agent that searches, books or buys on its site or app.

    Key facts: The terms also bar using data from United’s site or app, such as fares and schedules, to “train, fine-tune, ground, evaluate, or otherwise develop” an AI model. As of Nov. 14, United’s robots.txt named no AI crawlers or agents. Separately, HUMAN Security’s October report found that Meta’s and OpenAI’s agents made about 90% of the agent requests on sites and apps it protects.

    In HUMAN Security’s October data, Muse accounted for 59% of agent requests. Three OpenAI agents accounted for about 30% combined.

    Sources indicate that meta’s Muse publishes no user agent for a robots.txt rule to name, as Slobodan Manic wrote in October, so whether it gets in comes down to your terms and bot protection. Muse sent the most requests in HUMAN’s data, and bot rules can check the signatures some of its requests carry, whose key directory DataDome reported had moved to muse.ai by Nov. 9.

    Read our full coverage: United Lets Search Engines Index Its Site, Makes AI Agents Ask First and Meta & OpenAI Agents Made Nearly 90% Of Agent Requests In Bot Data.

    It has been revealed that much of this week’s SEO work sits with teams outside of SEO. The next steps for this week include identifying who is responsible for the off switch for the /random/ redirect, as well as reporting on the branded split and the analytics rules for referrers. Google’s CDN advice should be reviewed by whoever runs the CDN and firewall, and the automated calls toggle is managed through the Business Profile. United’s rules related to agents are contained within a legal agreement. Before the next change, the first step is to determine who has responsibility for each of these in your own organization.

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    In a recent development, kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    You'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, rolls out, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    Industry observers note that first Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing presently works at Kit.

    It has been revealed that first Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage currently routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action plan on how we can win these creators.

    First Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure rolls out that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a fresh tier or add-on (nice to have).

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth tech giant, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    In a recent development, preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    Senior Product Marketing Manager - Upmarket at Kit

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1744 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love.
    • It has been revealed that kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve.
    • You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    It has been revealed that kit's most established creators run real companies, with teams, large lists, dedicated sending needs, and a buying process that our self-serve motion wasn't built to serve. Because this part of our business is growing, we're looking for a Senior Product Marketing Manager, Scaling Creators to own how Kit wins, lands, and expands these businesses through a sales-assisted motion that sits alongside our self-serve product.

    You'll define who this buyer is, write the story that resonates and wins with them, and build the GTM strategy to drive inbound pipeline for our sales team. When these creators choose Kit and grow on it, they build more valuable businesses, and that's the outcome this role exists for.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led manufacturer before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

    You'll report to Christina Lhi, Head of Marketing, and work alongside two other experienced Product Marketing Managers on Kit's product marketing team. Together, you'll keep the self-serve and sales-assisted stories feeling like one Kit.

    You'll spend a lot of your time with:.

    Our sales leadership, on who we sell to, the deal toolkit, enablement, and win/loss.

    Account Executives and Solutions Consultants, on demo narratives, discovery, and technical and migration proof.

    Product, on packaging, introduces, and roadmap input.

    RevOps and analytics, on how accounts get routed to sales, attribution, and pricing decisions.

    Creator Success, on case studies, customer references, and expansion plays.

    Demand gen, content, and events, on campaigns and events for established creators.

    According to recent reports, first Week: Dive into our onboarding curriculum in Notion and learn Kit's product, pricing, and current positioning. Attend Get-To-Know-You (GTKY) meetings with marketing, sales, Solutions Consultants, RevOps, and Creator Success. Get access to our CRM, call recordings, and product analytics, and start listening to recent sales calls. Understand how product marketing at the moment works at Kit.

    First Month: Shadow 15+ sales calls and talk with 10 established creators, including recent wins, losses, and churned accounts. Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage at the moment routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them. And an action proposal on how we can win these creators.

    First Year: Sales runs on messaging and tools you built, pitch with confidence and we drive 2X inbound MQLs from when you started. You’ll own and lead our channel strategy, setting the vision, driving cross-functional alignment, and partnering with Marketing to bring it to life. You'll run a quarterly win/loss program and share what you learn openly, build a clear path for sales leads on our website, and make sure releases that matter to larger accounts ship with both a self-serve and a sales-assisted version. Your work has a direct impact on helping Kit reach $100,000,000 ARR while protecting the self-serve engine that got us here.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a upcoming tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth company, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    You lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    Sources indicate that you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    In a recent development, experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    Treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    Industry observers note that wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    Industry observers note that preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    According to recent reports, kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    We cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna.

    $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Organization-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    We usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

    A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    According to recent reports, we’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

    Kit is an equal opportunity employer.

    Recent findings suggest that we value diversity in all of its forms. Research tells us that applicants who are female or non-binary, as well as applicants who are people of color, are less likely to apply for roles they do not feel 100% qualified for. If you think you meet more than 50% of our requirements but fewer than 100% of them, please apply.

    We’re imperfect communicators, so think of our job postings as the starting point for discussion rather than proof that you shouldn’t apply.

    Kit does not discriminate on the basis of race, sex, color, religion, age, national origin, marital status, disability, veteran status, genetic information, sexual orientation, gender identity or any other reason prohibited by law in provision of employment opportunities and benefits.

    Segmentation and buyer definition: turning firmographic and product usage data into a clear picture of who to sell to and when.

    Messaging and positioning for a sales-assisted buyer, including competitive differentiation and objection handling.

    Sales enablement that reps actually use: demo narratives, discovery guides, business cases, and battlecards.

    Writing and storytelling that turns product depth into a business case a non-technical buyer can act on.

    Working with CRM, product analytics, and pipeline data to measure funnel conversion, win rate, and deal size.

    Customer and market/competitor research, including win/loss interviews and call analysis.

    Systems thinking: connecting people, processes, data, and tools to identify opportunities and build repeatable solutions across the go-to-market motion.

    Strong AI fluency: knowing when to leverage AI and how to build AI-powered workflows or tools that scale product marketing work, with human judgment and quality checks built in.

    Pricing and packaging input for a new tier or add-on (nice to have).

    7+ years in B2B SaaS product marketing, including at least 2 years supporting a sales team selling to mid-market and/or larger accounts.

    Added a sales-led motion on top of a product-led one at a high-growth organization, and can show what changed before and after with clear metrics.

    Built a deal toolkit and enablement program from little or nothing, and tied it to a sales metric like win rate or deal size.

    Ran a win/loss or customer research program that changed how a team sold or built.

    Ran an expansion or account-based program for an existing customer base (nice to have).

    Worked in email, martech, or the creator economy.

    You lead without a formal title. You align sales, product, RevOps, and finance on goals, trade-offs, and what success looks like, then keep things moving.

    You advocate for creators in decisions, and you protect the self-serve experience instead of pushing every account toward sales.

    You act with urgency and stay focused on hitting OKRs and owning outcomes.

    Sources indicate that you work in public. You share findings, drafts, and the reasoning behind decisions so others can build on them.

    You connect data to decisions, and you help others get sharper about using it.

    You raise the bar on quality and iterate toward it, and you shape how your team uses AI, from call analysis to keeping battlecards current.

    It has been revealed that experience in only self-serve or only enterprise sales. This role lives in the space between them, and you'll need to understand both.

    Industry observers note that treating enablement as a deck handoff. The work includes coaching reps, measuring what gets used, and revising what doesn't land.

    Industry observers note that wanting a sales playbook already in place. Much of this motion doesn't exist yet, and you'll be building it as you learn.

    Sources indicate that preferring to be measured on output rather than outcomes. You'll share accountability with Sales for win rate, deal size, and expansion revenue.

    Recent findings suggest that needing extensive approval before acting. You'll be trusted to make calls on speed versus quality and to explain your reasoning.

    Discomfort with direct, candid feedback, especially from sellers on what's working in live deals.

    It has been revealed that we're 100% remote with team members across the globe. We work mostly on East Coast time—so if you're based on the West Coast of the United States, Europe, or Asia, you might have a few early mornings or late evenings. We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. For this role, we’re hiring at our level 4 ($166,000). Level is determined based on experience and our interview process.

    Recent findings suggest that we cover up to $2,280 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance prepares through Aetna.

    Recent findings suggest that $2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Company-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget.

    Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year).

    Creator meetup budget ($50/month) to connect with creators over coffee, lunch, or other in-person meetups.

    Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON.

    Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment.

    Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work.

    Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days.

    Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year.

    Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months.

    Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period.

    Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team.

    Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year.

    It has been revealed that we usually receive a large number of applications, and our goal is to follow up with you within two weeks. You’ll hear from us either way. Here’s what you can expect from the rest of our hiring process:.

    A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min).

    Hiring manager interview (45 min).

    We’ll keep you informed through every step. To get started, complete this application, including a cover letter and answers to the questions on the next page. We read every single application, and your cover letter and responses help put your experience into context.

This role is ideal for someone who is building strong product management fundamentals, enjoys working closely with engineering and design, and is energized by keeping product work organized, well-documented, and moving toward release.

    Recent findings suggest that in this role, you will own specific product features or workstreams under the guidance of a Sr Technical Product Manager. You will help translate product intent into clear user stories, jobs-to-be-done, acceptance criteria, release aims, documentation, and operational updates. You will work across Product, Engineering, Design, Product Analytics, Customer Success, Sales, and Product Marketing to ensure product records are accurate, dependencies are visible, stakeholders are informed, and shipped work meets the expected customer and business outcomes.

    This role blends TPM expectations with the Delivery Product Owner operating model: the Sr TPM sets product direction, priorities, success metrics, and major tradeoffs; the TPM helps ensure that direction becomes shippable, well-understood, and well-supported product increments.

    An established social media following is a plus, but not required.

    #43825. Latest Update: WTF is a unified media platform?

    Latest Update: WTF is a unified media platform?

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2253 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • In a recent development, this article is a WTF explainer, in which we break down media and marketing’s most confusing terms.
    • Editor’s note: These technologies are ill-defined, please share feedback to “editorial@digiday.com” to talk more.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    In a recent development, this article is a WTF explainer, in which we break down media and marketing’s most confusing terms. More from the series →.

    Editor’s note: These technologies are ill-defined, please share feedback to “editorial@digiday.com” to talk more.

    Ad tech has never been short on acronyms. Its latest crop includes: unified advertising platforms (UAPs), unified media platforms (UMPs), and unified buying platforms (UBPs).

    This kind of language has added a upcoming layer of confusion to the space, and ad executives across adland have been saying, “WTF…?” Digiday is here to help by trying to bring some clarity to the matter.

    A simple way to approach the question is to think of such terms — UAP, UBP and UMP — as overlapping labels for technology that promises to make advertising easier to buy, manage and optimize across an increasingly fragmented media landscape.

    According to recent reports, of course, AI is central to the pitch. Advocates of such technologies maintain that instead of separately operating campaigns across Google, Meta, Amazon and the open web, advertisers could potentially use one system to determine where money goes, then execute those decisions through the relevant platforms.

    Some providers propose bringing buying and selling infrastructure together. Others want to sit above existing systems and coordinate them. This is an important distinction to keep in mind, as connective software is not the same as controlling how an advertiser spends its next dollar.

    In a recent development, at its simplest, a UMP coordinates planning, buying, optimization, and measurement across multiple media channels. Its remit could include programmatic display, CTV, retail media, search, social, and direct publisher relationships.

    According to most sources, the idea is not necessarily to replace every existing media trading infrastructure, i.e., demand-side and supply-side platforms, etc., but to make them work together more efficiently.

    That is distinct from the traditional remit of a DSP, many of which have spent years expanding the inventory and formats available through their own buying interfaces. A unified platform, by contrast, promises to operate across buying environments that no single DSP controls.

    According to recent reports, jay Friedman, co-founder of CartographAI, told Digiday that the emerging proposition is about budget fluidity, not simply consolidating DSPs and SSPs. “We define a UMP as a platform that executes buys across all primary digital channels (search, social, programmatic, and direct). This may or may not include agents,” Friedman told Digiday. “Traditionally, this has been the domain of agency order management systems,” he said, noting how several newly introduced entrants are hoping to challenge these players.

    In a recent development, the terms overlap, but they differ in what they promise to unify. The chart below traces that range, from handling an individual transaction to coordinating campaigns across channels and deciding where budgets go.

    Keith Weisberg of Unplugged Collective told Digiday UBPs would initially come to market as a repackaging of existing tools. He noted the deeper shift would come when buyers could bring their data to the places ads run and delegate spending decisions to AI agents.

    In a recent development, “I’d treat that as a net-new product, not a DSP feature,” he said. “However, we’re all plugged into DSPs, and even if it’s a new product, it’ll roll out via our current commercial relationships, because that trust (and legal contracting) took years.”.

    Ana Milicevic, co-founder of Sparrow Advisers, described the labels as directional distinctions rather than settled product categories. She added, “It’s not all just a collection of black boxes. Then that’s a net latest layer in the stack.” The key distinction is whether a platform merely pushes buttons in existing interfaces or makes independent decisions about where budgets go.

    Industry observers note that ciarán O’Kane, general partner at First Party Capital, was more skeptical about novelty. In wording expressly cleared for attribution, he characterized UMPs and UBPs as “meta DSPs” that act as workflow layers on top of existing systems by plugging into APIs. He also said many emerging players in the space that use this terminology are revisiting approaches the industry has tried before.

    Media-buying teams have long struggled with the fragmentation of conducting ad campaigns using different buying interfaces, datasets, and measurement methods. AI can make the operational work of combining and interpreting those inputs less expensive, but it does not automatically create comparable performance data or independent buying authority.

    According to recent reports, “The frustration is very, very old. What’s newly introduced now is that AI is letting us operationally skip through some hurdles that were previously insurmountable,” Milicevic told Digiday. Tasks that once demanded a substantial analytics stack and specialist labor can increasingly be assisted by repeatable prompts and automated processes.

    The commercial question is whether cheaper orchestration creates an entirely newly introduced buyer or simply a more convenient way to operate existing platforms. For advertisers, that distinction determines whether the new technology saves money, reallocates money, or merely adds another vendor to pay.

    It has been revealed that in an Oct. 8 blog post, titled “universal buying platform,” Apostrophe co-founders Brian O’Kelley and Anne Coghlan outlined a broader buying layer intended to connect intent, execution, and measurement across advertising environments, citing the recent launch of Amazon Ads Agent as an example of this trend.

    Their argument is a public proposal, not evidence that a single independent platform already performs every part of the workflow at scale — O’Kelley did not respond to Digiday’s request for comment by press time.

    Other companies are approaching the problem from different directions, with Olyzon — an entity that used the term “agentic orchestration platform” in its recent CTV launch material — serving as one example.

    Jules Minvielle, co-founder and CEO of Olyzon, told Digiday the tech giant does not own inventory and uses agents to coordinate buying through existing platforms, with advertiser-controlled approvals. “A DSP is one place where you can buy. Orchestration is all the work around the buy: building the blueprint, deciding where each dollar goes, activating across every platform, watching delivery, measuring, and feeding what worked into the next plan,” he wrote in an emailed statement, adding that uneven API access and inconsistent measurement remain substantial obstacles.

    Sources indicate that ravi Patel, co-founder and CEO of SWYM.ai, drew a distinction between a common interface and control over the budget. “It can manage the ‘what’ and the ‘how much.’ It can’t manage the ‘which impression.’ That distinction is the whole story,” he explained, adding that campaign setup and pacing across platforms are already possible through APIs. However, impression-level optimization within the major walled gardens remains in their own systems.

    Recent findings suggest that lucas Cridland, CEO of Basin Media, questioned whether agents are changing the underlying buying process. “At the moment, many environments are agentically operating in the same supply chain flow. They’re just doing it with agents buying; they’re not radically changing the way the process works. And that’s where the real edge exists.”.

    Recent findings suggest that not necessarily. Many of the newly introduced propositions depend on DSPs continuing to execute transactions, access inventory, and optimize within their own environments. The change may be who decides which platform gets the advertiser’s budget in the first place.

    Milicevic maintained that “value always accrues to whoever is closest to the decision or outright owns the decision.”.

    Ergo, if DSPs cannot move upstream into genuine cross-channel decision-making, they risk becoming “dumb pipes,” i.e., a commoditized, essential infrastructure whose underlying value is less visible to buyers.

    Incumbent DSPs, however, have established advertiser relationships, bidding technology, data integrations and scale. They could develop their own orchestration capabilities. A new intermediary would need to show that its independence produces better decisions, rather than simply adding another fee, according to several sources consulted for this piece.

    Industry observers note that agencies already coordinate campaigns across channels, negotiate buying arrangements and manage the systems needed to execute them. Friedman, a former long-time agency-lead, argued that unified platforms could challenge agency order-management systems while bringing neglected channels, including creator-led media, into a common workflow.

    Such a scenario would not eliminate strategic planning, creative development, or oversight, but it could change how much manual campaign administration agencies perform, where they develop proprietary expertise, and which services clients are willing to pay for, with AI at the center of many contractual renegotiations between advertisers and media agencies.

    Such a scenario would not eliminate strategic planning, creative development, or oversight, but it could change how much manual campaign administration agencies perform, where they develop proprietary expertise, and which services clients are willing to pay for, with AI at the center of many contractual renegotiations between advertisers and media agencies.

    In a recent development, the biggest obstacle may be the very platforms that independent systems are supposed to coordinate. Google, Meta, and Amazon control their own buying tools, data, and optimization systems. Access through an API does not necessarily provide the granular information or authority required to compare results and independently move budgets.

    Trust is also an issue. A unified interface can display reports from multiple platforms without proving that the outcomes are comparable. Attribution windows, campaign objectives, and self-reported measurement differ across channels, meaning an independent buying layer needs a credible basis for deciding that one dollar is better spent in one environment than another.

    Friedman was skeptical that interoperability would resolve the underlying problems, and highlighted how Google and Meta are unlikely to make their systems interoperable. He further questioned whether agencies could build the context and routing infrastructure needed to translate employees’ instructions into accurate buying decisions, even if every platform supported the Model Context Protocol. “Interoperability won’t solve anything,” he told Digiday.

    Greg MacDonald, founder of Chelsea Strategies, noted addressing media buying’s growing complexity could reduce spending on its mechanics and, over time, potentially improve advertiser outcomes. However, he remained cautious about how far unified platforms could go. “I’m skeptical that the walled gardens will give buyers more control than they have today,” he told Digiday, pointing to persistent difficulties with frequency capping across programmatic formats, let alone disconnected marketplaces.

    “But you don’t have to solve every problem, and certainly not on day one to be useful,” MacDonald added. He compared the opportunity with programmatic guaranteed buying, which made the insertion-order process more efficient without fundamentally changing direct media buying.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, Milicevic said the more plausible near-term customer may be a multichannel advertiser between the largest global brands and small businesses that largely rely on a single platform. She also stressed the need for independent validation of results, rather than taking each platform’s own reporting at face value.

    AI agents could help automate campaign setup, inventory discovery, negotiation, execution, and reporting. That makes agentic advertising relevant to the unified-platform debate, but not synonymous with it: automating tasks is different from making accountable, cross-channel budget decisions.

    According to recent reports, unplugged Collective maps seven ways AI could change advertising (see graphic below). Per Weisberg, two are central to the unified buying debate: how agents decide where to spend and how they carry out those decisions across platforms.

    Sources indicate that industry initiatives such as AdCP and IAB Tech Lab’s agentic work aim to establish ways for systems to communicate and execute workflows. Technical standards could reduce integration costs, but they cannot by themselves force walled gardens to disclose comparable data or surrender commercial control.

    Seasoned industry observers have seen enough buzz phrases come and go to feel confident enough to make tongue-in-cheek observations when a latest acronym becomes de rigueur among the industry’s chattering classes.

    “I saw ‘UMP’ and I thought: ad network,” quipped Terence Kawaja, CEO, LUMA Partners, a prominent investment bank in the space, speaking on stage at this year’s Prebid Summit – channeling the industry adage, “everything is an ad network.”.

    Meanwhile, one prominent industry source, who requested anonymity to preserve industry relationships, dismissed the latest acronyms as another serving of “word salad.” However, the barbs, playful or otherwise, raise a palpable industry debate: As AI makes it cheaper to run campaigns across platforms, who gets to decide where the money goes?

    The clearest test is whether advertisers entrust meaningful cross-channel allocation to an independent system — and can demonstrate that the decisions improve outcomes. Smaller-scale automation and campaign management do not, on their own, prove that a new market category has emerged.

    Milicevic identified three indicators: real advertiser budgets moving under independent allocation, credible measurement outside any single walled garden, and changes in how marketing organizations structure teams. “If it’s truly structural, it’ll show up in the PNL, and if it’s slideware and fluff, then that’ll make its way into award entries and kind of the PR circuit,” she stated.

    Industry observers note that for now, the most useful distinction is between controlling the infrastructure through which ads are purchased and controlling the decision about where the money goes. The latter is the more ambitious promise. Whether anyone can deliver it independently, at scale, and at a cost advertisers will accept remains unresolved.

    After 45 years of negotiating, the chairman of Publicis Media Exchange (PMX) U.S., is stepping down from a full-time role this year, although he aims to continue to consult with the holdco.

    Mediaplus and Publicis clients, including Banco Santander, have paused TikTok spending in wake of investigations into abuse images circulating on the video platform.

    Madison and Wall estimates creator marketing growing at double the pace of the rest of advertising, driven on by creator-led production investments.
